title: Selling an inherited house taxes
description: Selling an inherited house taxes start with basis in IRS Publication 523, not the decedent's old purchase price. Not legal or tax advice.
summary: Ask what the basis is on the date-of-death rules in Publication 523 before anyone spends the proceeds.
body: This is not legal or tax advice. Selling an inherited house taxes is a federal question [IRS Publication 523](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p523) addresses in its basis section, and a state question this page does not. The publication says that if you inherited your home from someone who died before or after 2010, your basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or a later alternate valuation date if the estate chose one. A death in 2010 has its own discussion. Do not file from a summary.

The old purchase price is usually the wrong start. Gain is the difference between the amount realized on your sale and that inherited basis, after the selling costs the publication allows. If you sell soon after the death for a price near the date-of-death value, the gain may be small. It is not automatically zero. A preparer computes it. Depreciation, a rental history, or a gift instead of an inheritance changes the file.

The main-home exclusion is a separate test about the seller's own use. Heirs do not automatically receive the decedent's exclusion. An heir who also lived in the house may have their own tests. A surviving spouse should read the publication's community-property and joint-ownership pages. Texas is on the publication's community-property list. Bring the appraisal and the closing statement to the preparer before the proceeds are divided and spent.

Who signs the deed is not a tax question. If you are not sure you may sell, stop and read the probate and trust notes. Paying tax on a sale you were not allowed to make is a worse problem than a late return. Keep the folder for the period the IRS recordkeeping page describes.
steps: Read the inherited-home basis section of Publication 523.
Get a value as of the date of death, or the alternate date if the estate used one.
Do not start from the decedent's old purchase price.
Ask a preparer about the exclusion before you assume it applies to the heirs.
Keep the appraisal and the closing statement together.

title: Selling a house in a trust after death
description: Selling a house in a trust after death depends on the deed and the trust. A trustee may sell, or the house may still be in the estate.
summary: Read the deed and the trust together. A house people call a trust house is sometimes still in the decedent's name.
body: This is not legal or tax advice. Selling a house in a trust after death starts with two documents: the deed and the trust. If the deed is in the trustee's name, the successor trustee named in the trust may be the person who can list and sign, once a title company accepts the papers. If the deed is still in the decedent's own name, the trust was never funded for this house, and the estate may have to act. People use the word trust for both situations. The title company will not.

Read who becomes trustee at death and what they must record. A death certificate may be enough, or a lawyer may tell you a further step remains. Do not list the house because you are the person who has the keys. Ask the title company which letters they need before they will insure a buyer. That question is cheaper than a contract you cannot close.

The other people who benefit still need the trust's instructions on notice and on how money is divided. Agree in writing before a buyer is in the driveway. A fight about the refrigerator is easier than a fight about the signer. Tax basis is the other topic. Publication 523 still applies to the sale. This note does not compute the gain. It only gets the correct person to the listing appointment.

When the signer is clear, use the ordinary prep, pricing, and closing guides. Authority first. Paint second. If a mortgage or a reverse mortgage remains, order a payoff quote. The lien does not disappear because the owner died.
steps: Read the current deed and the trust, not a memory of what someone intended.
Identify the successor trustee and the proof a title company wants.
If the deed is in the decedent's name, ask a lawyer whether probate is still required.
Write down what the beneficiaries agreed before you list.
Order any loan payoff only after you know who may request it.

title: Selling parents house after death
description: Selling parents house after death starts with who may sign, then insurance, papers, and a date-of-death value. Not legal or tax advice.
summary: Secure the house and find the signer before you clean it out or promise a buyer a date.
body: This is not legal or tax advice. Selling parents house after death is usually several people, one house, and one person who is actually allowed to sign. Find the will, the trust, and any court paper before you call an agent. The child who lives nearest is often the one who gets the calls. Nearness is not authority. A title company will ask for letters or a trustee's documents. Get that list in the first week.

Tell the insurer the owner died and ask what the policy covers while the house is empty. Keep heat or cooling on if the policy or the weather requires it. Change the locks only if the lawyer says you may, and not against someone who still has a right to enter. Do not empty the house into a dumpster. Improvement receipts and tax papers are the basis file. [IRS Publication 523](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p523) is why those papers matter even when the starting basis is a date-of-death value.

Talk to the other heirs before you pick a price. Write what you agreed. A list price one person loves and another will not sign is not a list price. If a court is involved, you may not be allowed to accept an offer yet. The probate note is that question. If a trust owns the house, the trust note is the question. This page is the family version: slow down, name the signer, keep the papers.

After authority is clear, the house is an ordinary sale. Walk it with the prep guide. Disclose what you know. Do not guess at repairs a parent mentioned once. If you do not know, say you do not know and get a look, rather than answering a form from childhood memory.
steps: Find the will, the trust, and any probate papers.
Ask a title company who must sign.
Insure the empty house and stop the clean-out until papers are saved.
Agree with the other heirs in writing before you list.
Use the ordinary selling guides only after the signer is clear.

title: Probate sale of a house
description: A probate sale of a house may need a court step or an independent executor's authority. Ask a local lawyer before you advertise a closing date.
summary: Confirm the estate can deliver a deed on the date you want before you accept an offer.
body: This is not legal or tax advice. A probate sale of a house is a sale while a court file is open, or a sale by an executor the court has recognized. States differ. Some estates are independent and can sell without asking permission for each step. Some need an order, a waiting period, or a particular notice. A lawyer in the state where the house sits is the person who knows which sentence is yours. This site will not rank the states.

Ask the title company, early, what they need to insure the deed: letters testamentary, a court order, or something else. If they cannot insure it, a buyer cannot close on the date in a cheerful listing. Do not advertise a closing three weeks out because that is when the buyer wants to move. Advertise a date the estate can actually meet.

Price and repairs still matter, and they wait on authority. An empty house can still leak. Keep it insured and ask before you spend estate money on a remodel. Heirs sometimes want improvements that the estate should not buy. Write the decision down. The prep guide is the order of work once spending is allowed.

Tax reporting for the estate and for the heirs can both exist. Publication 523 covers the basis of an inherited home. An estate's income tax return is a preparer's job. Do not distribute the sale proceeds the afternoon of closing if the lawyer or the accountant told you to wait for expenses and taxes. The wire is not a gift to divide in the parking lot. Ask the lawyer what you may spend while the case is open before you hire a crew.
steps: Ask a local probate lawyer whether this estate can sell without a further court order.
Ask the title company which papers they will require.
Set the closing date only after those answers exist.
Keep the house insured while the case is open.
Do not distribute proceeds until the lawyer or accountant says the estate can.

title: Step up in basis inherited house
description: A step up in basis on an inherited house generally uses fair market value at death, as IRS Publication 523 describes. Not tax advice.
summary: Publication 523 points inherited basis at the date-of-death value, with an alternate date and a 2010 exception to read carefully.
body: This is not tax advice. A step up in basis inherited house is the common name for a rule [IRS Publication 523](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p523) states more carefully. If you inherited the home from someone who died before or after 2010, your basis is the fair market value on the date of death, or the later alternate valuation date chosen by the estate's personal representative. If a federal estate tax return was filed or required, the value on that return matters. A death in 2010 is a different section. Read it before you apply the sentence.

The practical paper is an appraisal or other support for that date-of-death value, ordered while the condition of the house is still the condition on that date. A value you invent from a website a year later is a weak file. Selling costs and later improvements still adjust the math. The old purchase price is not the starting point for a true inheritance. A gift uses different rules, also in the publication. Do not call a gift an inheritance because it happened near a death.

Community property has another page in the publication. Texas is on that list. A surviving spouse's basis can change for the whole property when the conditions are met, not only for half. A preparer applies the conditions. This note only tells you the page exists so you do not use a joint-tenant example from a different state.

Keep the appraisal with the closing statement. The records note explains how long to hold the file. The exclusion for a main home is not the same as a step-up. You can have a stepped-up basis and still need to ask whether any gain above that basis is excluded. Run both questions. Do not skip one because the other sounds favorable.
steps: Read the inherited-basis paragraphs in Publication 523, including the 2010 note.
Support the date-of-death value with an appraisal or the estate return.
Do not use a gift basis or the old purchase price by habit.
If the house is community property, have a preparer read that section.
File the appraisal with the sale records.
